transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

I’ve gotten stuck doing these little routines. I’ll wash my hands again after I handle my wrist brace, check the stove and the front door over and over, and silently count through steps before I leave. I know I’ve already done enough, but it’s starting to make me late.
Before you do one of these routines, do you get an unwanted thought or fear that pushes you to do it?

Yes. It’s like an ugly little thought barges in that I’ve left something unsafe, or touched something unclean, or somehow put somebody at risk. I know it’s out of proportion, but it keeps nagging at me until I do the routine.
When those thoughts pop in, do they feel like your own thoughts, even though they’re unwanted?

Yes, they do feel like my own thoughts. I’ll be reading at home or getting ready for a museum shift, and this ugly thought just barges in—like I’ve left something unsafe or touched something unclean, or put someone at risk. I know it’s out of proportion, but it still gets stuck there.
When you do the routine, does your anxiety go down afterward?
Yes, usually it does, at least for a little while. After I wash or check again, I can move on—but then I start wondering if I did it properly, and I end up going back.
Besides the routines, do you also have these unwanted thoughts even at times when you do not act on them?

Yes. They can come up when I’m just reading at home or getting ready for my museum shift. It’s that same thought that I’ve left something unsafe, touched something unclean, or put someone at risk. I know it’s out of proportion, but it still barges in.
Do you feel these fears and routines are unreasonable or excessive?

Yes. I know I’ve already done enough, but I still wash again after handling my wrist brace, or go back to check the stove and front door. I even silently count through the steps before I leave. It feels excessive, especially when it makes me late.
When you wash your hands after handling your wrist brace, is it mainly because you feel contaminated?
Yes, mostly. After I handle the wrist brace, I feel like I need to wash my hands again, even though I know I’ve already done enough.
When you silently count through the steps before you leave, is it because things do not feel complete or 'just right' until you do?
Yes. I feel like I have to count through it before I can leave, even though I know I’ve already checked. Otherwise it doesn’t feel settled, and I end up delayed.
Which troubles you more overall: the unwanted intrusive thoughts, or the rituals like washing, checking, and counting?
The rituals, I think. The washing, going back to check the stove and door, counting before I leave—those are what keep me stuck and make me late, even though I know I’ve done enough.
On a typical day, do these rituals and intrusive thoughts take more than an hour altogether?

Yes, I think it can add up to more than an hour, especially when I’m trying to get out the door. I’m still managing on my own, but it’s made me late for docent shifts, and I’ve skipped a few museum events because leaving feels like too much.
Do the unwanted intrusive thoughts bother you more than the rituals, or less?

Less, I’d say. The thoughts are upsetting—they’ll pop in while I’m reading or getting ready, that I’ve left something unsafe or put someone at risk—but I know they’re out of proportion. It’s the rituals afterward that take up more of my time.
If you were somehow prevented from doing the washing, checking, or counting, would the unwanted thoughts still keep bothering you a lot on their own?

Yes, they probably would. Even if I couldn’t do the washing or checking, those thoughts would still barge in—like when I’m reading or getting ready to go to the museum—that I’ve left something unsafe or somehow put someone at risk. I know it’s out of proportion, but it’s still upsetting.
When the intrusive thoughts come up, are they themselves very distressing to you?

Yes, they are upsetting. I’ll be reading at home or getting ready for a museum shift, and this thought will barge in that I’ve left something unsafe, touched something unclean, or put someone at risk. I know it’s out of proportion, but it still bothers me.
Outside of these contamination, checking, and counting concerns, do you also spend a lot of time worrying about many other parts of life?
I’m not sure I’d say I spend a lot of time worrying about lots of other things. It’s mainly these particular concerns that get stuck in my head.
Have these symptoms been present most of your adult life, as part of your usual way of being?
I’m not really sure. I haven’t thought of it as being part of my usual way of being for most of my adult life.
Overall, would you say your symptoms are mostly the repetitive rituals, mostly the intrusive thoughts, or both about equally?

Mostly the rituals, I think. I get caught up washing again, checking the stove and door, or counting through what I need to do before I leave. I know I’ve done enough, but I still repeat it, and it can make me late.
When you are not doing the washing, checking, or counting, do these intrusive thoughts take up a lot of time by themselves?

Yes, sometimes they do. I’ll be reading at home or getting ready for a museum shift, and this unpleasant thought keeps popping in that I left something unsafe, touched something unclean, or put someone at risk. I know it’s out of proportion, but it can keep barging back in.
Would you say the intrusive thoughts and the rituals bother you about equally?
The rituals bother me more. It’s the washing, rechecking the stove and door, and counting through things before I leave—they can hold me up even when I know I’ve already done enough.
When you are not doing the washing, checking, or counting, do the intrusive thoughts bother you nearly as much as the rituals do?

Not nearly as much, no. They do bother me—an ugly thought will pop up that I’ve left something unsafe or contaminated, or that I’ve put someone at risk—but I know it’s out of proportion. The rituals are what really hold me up.
